      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> Lymphoma</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> <span class="qt1">Disease</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma? <p><span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma, also called <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> <span class="qt1">disease</span>, is a type of cancer that develops in the lymph system. Your lymph system is part of your immune system. It helps protect your body from infection and <span class="qt1">disease</span>.</p><p>The lymph system is made up of tissues and organs that produce, store, and carry white blood cells. It includes your:</p><ul><li>Bone marrow</li><li>Lymph nodes</li><li>Lymphatic vessels</li><li>Spleen</li><li>Thymus</li><li>Tonsils</li></ul><p><span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma is one of the main types of lymphoma. The other is non-<span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma. Each type starts in different types of white blood cells.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma?<p>The cause of <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma is unknown. But there are certain people who are at higher risk of developing it.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma?<p>Certain factors can make you more likely to develop <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma:</p><ul><li>Age. <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma is most common in early adulthood (age 20-39 years) and in late adulthood (age 65 years and older).</li><li>Being male. The risk of adult <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma is slightly higher in males than in females.</li><li>Past Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. Having an infection with EBV as a young child or teenager increases your risk of <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma.</li><li>A family history of <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma. Having a parent or sibling with <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma increases your risk of developing it.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma?<p>The signs and symptoms of <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma may include:</p><ul><li>Painless, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, or groin</li><li>Fever for no known reason</li><li>Drenching night sweats (very heavy sweating during sleep)</li><li>Weight loss for no known reason in the past 6 months</li><li>Itchy skin, especially after bathing or drinking alcohol</li><li>Fatigue</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma, your provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms and medical history. This will include checking for signs of <span class="qt1">disease</span>, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual.</li><li>May order some lab tests, such as:
  <ul><li>Complete blood count</li><li>Blood chemistry studies</li><li>Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) test</li><li>Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) test</li><li>Blood tests to rule out other medical conditions</li><li>May do imaging tests such as a CT and PET (positron emission tomography) scans</li><li>May do a lymph node biopsy</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma?<p>Treatments for <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma include:</p><ul><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells</li><li>Cancer immunotherapy</li></ul><p><span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma can usually be cured if it is found and treated early.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/lymphoma.html">
      <content name="title">Lymphoma</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Non-<span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> Lymphoma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Waldenstrom's Macroglobulinemia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Lymphoma is a cancer of a part of the immune system called the lymph system.  There are many types of lymphoma.  One type is <span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> <span class="qt1">disease</span>.  The rest are called non-<span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphomas.</p><p>Non-<span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphomas begin when a type of white blood cell, called a T cell or B cell, becomes abnormal. The cell divides again and again, making more and more abnormal cells. These abnormal cells can spread to almost any other part of the body. Most of the time, doctors don't know why a person gets non-<span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma. You are at increased risk if you have a weakened immune system or have certain types of infections.</p><p>Non-<span class="qt0">Hodgkin</span> lymphoma can cause many symptoms, such as :</p><ul><li>Swollen, painless lymph nodes in the neck, armpits or groin</li><li>Unexplained weight loss </li><li>Fever </li><li>Soaking night sweats </li><li>Coughing, trouble breathing or chest pain </li><li>Weakness and tiredness that don't go away </li><li>Pain, swelling or a feeling of fullness in the abdomen </li></ul><p>Your doctor will diagnose lymphoma with a physical exam, blood tests, a chest x-ray, and a biopsy.  Treatments include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, biological therapy, or therapy to remove proteins from the blood. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells. Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight cancer. If you don't have symptoms, you may not need treatment right away. This is called watchful waiting.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/tumorsandpregnancy.html">
      <content name="title">Tumors and Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cancer and Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Gestational Trophoblastic <span class="qt1">Disease</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Molar Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Tumors during pregnancy are rare, but they can happen. Tumors can be either benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). The most common cancers in pregnancy include breast cancer, thyroid cancer, cervical cancer, lymphoma, and melanoma.  Cancer itself rarely harms the fetus, and some cancer treatments are safe during pregnancy.  You and your health care provider will work together to find the best treatment.  Your choices will depend on how far along the pregnancy is, as well as the type, size, and stage of your cancer.</p><p>Another type of tumor that women can get is called a gestational trophoblastic <span class="qt1">disease</span> (GTD). It happens when a fertilized egg doesn't become a fetus.  GTD is not always easy to find. It is usually benign, but some types can be malignant. The most common type of GTD is a molar pregnancy. In its early stages, it may look like a normal pregnancy. You should see your provider if you have vaginal bleeding (not menstrual bleeding).</p><p>Treatment depends on the type of tumor, whether it has spread to other places, and your overall health.</p></content>
